client: Lately, I’ve been really anxious about failing to meet the deadline for my final university project. I keep worrying that it’s going to tank my overall grade and ruin all the hard work I’ve put in this semester. To be honest, I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like the damage is already done, and I don’t know how to stop spiraling about it.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of weight from this fear of falling short, and your voice reflects how overwhelming this feels right now. Let’s take a moment to untangle those thoughts—what evidence do you have that missing the deadline will *definitely* ruin everything, versus it being a possibility you’re focusing on? Sometimes, when we’re stuck in that spiral, it’s hard to see other paths forward, but they’re often there.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the evidence is that my professor has been really strict about deadlines in the past, and I’ve seen classmates fail assignments for turning things in late. It feels like there’s no room for error, and that’s why I’m so panicked. I’m not sure how to see other paths forward—it feels like the stakes are just too high.
therapist: Your worry about the professor’s strictness and your classmates’ experiences makes a lot of sense, especially when the stakes feel so high. It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of tension in this moment—your voice seems to reflect that urgency and fear. Let’s pause and consider: have there been times when you’ve faced tight deadlines before and still managed to pull through? Sometimes, our minds focus so much on the worst-case scenario that we forget our own resilience.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I’ve pulled through tight deadlines before, but this time feels different because the project is much bigger and more complex. I’ve been procrastinating a lot, and now I’m so behind that it’s hard to imagine catching up. Even if I do manage to finish, I’m worried the quality will suffer, and that just adds to the pressure.
therapist: It sounds like this project feels especially daunting because of its scale and complexity, and your voice reflects how heavy this burden feels right now. Procrastination often stems from feeling overwhelmed, and it’s not uncommon to get stuck in that cycle of worry and delay. Let’s break this down together—what’s one small, manageable step you could take today to start moving forward? Sometimes, focusing on just the next action can ease that sense of being buried under it all.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I could try writing just one section of the project today, but I'm worried even that might not be good enough. The perfectionist part of me keeps saying if I can't do it perfectly, there's no point starting. And honestly, when I sit down to work, my mind just goes blank from all the pressure.
therapist: That perfectionist voice can be so loud—it sounds like it’s not just criticizing your work, but also freezing you before you even begin. Your tone has a hint of exhaustion, like you’re drained from wrestling with these thoughts. What if we shifted focus from "perfect" to "progress"? Even a rough draft of one section is still movement forward, and that’s worth acknowledging. How would it feel to give yourself permission to write badly first, just to break the cycle?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try writing badly first, but it feels uncomfortable to let go of that perfectionist standard. What if I end up with something so messy that I can’t fix it later? The idea of progress over perfection makes sense in theory, but in practice, it’s hard to shake the fear of producing something subpar.
therapist: It sounds like letting go of that perfectionist standard feels really vulnerable—your voice carries a mix of hesitation and concern, almost like you’re bracing for disappointment. It’s understandable to feel uneasy about starting messy, especially when you’re used to holding yourself to such high expectations. What if we reframe "subpar" as "a stepping stone"? Every draft, even the messy ones, is part of the process, not the final product. How might it feel to experiment with that mindset, even just for today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I can try seeing the first draft as just a stepping stone, but part of me still worries the professor will judge me harshly even for early versions. And honestly, when I think about showing imperfect work, my chest gets tight - it feels like revealing something shameful. Maybe I could try writing just one messy paragraph today, but I'm not sure it'll actually help ease the pressure long-term.
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of writing one imperfect paragraph brings up a lot of discomfort—your voice has a quiet tension to it, as if the shame feels almost physical. That fear of the professor’s judgment runs deep, doesn’t it? Let’s notice how the mind is treating this first draft like it’s a final judgment on your worth, rather than what it actually is: a normal, necessary part of the process. What would it feel like to treat this paragraph as an experiment—not about the outcome, but about testing whether you can tolerate a little imperfection?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Treating it as an experiment feels a little less scary, but I’m still not sure I can fully let go of the fear of judgment. What if I start writing and the words are so bad that I can’t even look at them later? It’s hard to imagine tolerating imperfection when it feels like everything is riding on this project.
therapist: It sounds like even with the idea of an experiment, there’s still a lot of fear lingering—your voice seems to rise with worry, almost like the thought of bad words feels like a threat. That’s understandable when the stakes feel so high, and it’s okay to acknowledge how hard it is to sit with imperfection. What if we focus on curiosity instead of judgment? Imagine writing that paragraph as if you’re just observing what comes out, without needing to label it as "good" or "bad"—almost like you’re watching the process unfold from a distance. How does that feel to consider?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Trying to observe without judging sounds... interesting, but I don't know if I can actually do it. My brain automatically labels everything as good or bad writing. Maybe I could try for five minutes, but I still think I'll end up hating whatever I write - that's just how I've always been with my work.
therapist: It sounds like this feels like a big leap for you—your words and tone carry a mix of curiosity and skepticism, almost like you’re cautiously testing the idea but bracing for disappointment. That automatic labeling of "good" or "bad" is a deeply ingrained habit, and it’s okay if it doesn’t shift overnight. Starting with just five minutes of non-judgmental observation is a great step—it’s not about getting it "right," but about gently challenging that automatic judgment. Would you be open to trying it and seeing what happens, even if it feels uncomfortable at first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay... I'll try the five minutes, but I'm already thinking I'll probably delete whatever I write immediately after. It's just hard to believe this will help when the pressure is still there—I still need to turn in something good eventually. Maybe this is just avoiding the real issue, which is that I'm running out of time.
therapist: It sounds like even as you’re willing to try, there’s a lot of doubt lingering—your voice seems quieter and rushed, like you’re already anticipating disappointment. It’s understandable to feel like this might not be enough, especially with the clock ticking. But sometimes, starting small isn’t about avoiding the issue—it’s about creating a bit of space to breathe and move forward, even when the pressure feels overwhelming. What if we focus on this as a way to gently ease into the process, rather than expecting it to fix everything all at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess easing into the process makes sense, but it’s still hard to shake the feeling that I’m wasting time by not diving straight into fixing everything. I’m worried that even if I do this exercise, I’ll still end up overwhelmed later because the deadline is still looming. It’s like no matter what I try, the pressure is still there, and it’s hard to believe anything will make a difference.
therapist: It sounds like even as you consider easing into the process, there’s a real sense of urgency—your voice sounds tense and quick, like you’re already bracing for that overwhelming rush later. That fear of wasting time is so loud, isn’t it? But sometimes, what feels like "not enough" in the moment—like small steps—is actually what builds momentum. What if we focus on just this one exercise for now, and see how it feels, rather than trying to solve the entire looming deadline at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
